topics.description: The monarchical title and office held by the rulers of Russia, including the Russian Empire, until Nicholas II’s abdication in 1917.

parts.label: L
parts.question: The last ruler with this title was overthrown by the Bolsheviks. For ten points each,

parts.label: A
parts.question: Give this title for rulers of Russia prior to the October Revolution. The last man to hold this title was Nicholas II, who was executed along with his family.
parts.answer: Tsar (accept Czar)

parts.label: B
parts.question: This youngest daughter of Nicholas II was rumored to have survived the royal family’s execution. Many women impersonated this girl in attempts to claim her fortune.
parts.answer: Anastasia Romanov (accept Anastasiya Nikolayevna Romanov; prompt on “Romanov”)

parts.label: C
parts.question: This mystic and advisor to Nicholas II avoided being executed along with the imperial family because he had already been poisoned, stabbed, shot, and drowned.
parts.answer: Grigori Rasputin (accept Grigori Yefimovich Rasputin; accept Grigori Novykh)

parts.label: tossup
parts.question: After one holder of this position killed his son with a scepter in a fit of rage, this position saw a period of  instability that ended the Rurikid Dynasty’s control of it. Boris Gundunov was elected to this position before  the Time of Troubles, during which it was claimed by three (*) False Dmitrys. The last holder of this position  was forced to abdicate in the February Revolution of 1917, ending the Romanov Dynasty. For 10 points, identify  this royal position that ruled imperial Russia.
parts.answer: Tsar [or Czar; prompt on Ruler of Russia]

topics.description: Yugoslav communist leader who broke with Stalin, promoted brotherhood and unity and workers' self-management, and helped establish the Non-Aligned Movement.

parts.label: tossup
parts.question: Political prisoners in this country were held in a labor camp located on the island of Goli Otok. A leader of this country promoted the slogan “Brotherhood and unity” among this country’s various ethnic groups. This country became a republic after its last king, Peter II, was deposed following World War II. A leader of this country initiated its (*) Informbiro period following a split with the Soviet Union. That leader of this country served as the first chairman of the Non-Aligned Movement, of which this country was the only European founding member. This country was led by Slobodan Milosevic during its violent breakup in the 1990s. For 10 points, Josip Broz Tito led what former country located in the Balkans?
parts.answer: Yugoslavia [or Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia or Kingdom of Yugoslavia]

parts.label: tossup
parts.question: This country was organized into communes called opštine under a system called “workers’ self￾management.” This country’s Informbiro period followed World War II, during which the royalist Chetnik movement and the fascist Ustaše [oo-stah-sha] operated. A leader of this country who threatened “If you don’t stop sending killers, I’ll send one to Moscow” was the only European signee at the Bandung Conference for the (*) Non-Aligned Movement. This country fell apart when Slobodan Milošević [mil-OH-suh-VICH] rejected self-determination for Slovenes and Croats in the 1990s. Josip Broz Tito was the Cold War leader of, for 10 points, what former Balkan country?
parts.answer: Yugoslavia [accept Kingdom of Yugoslavia; or Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia; or Federal People’s Republic of Yugoslavia; accept Yugoslav Wars]

topics.description: Self-governing or semi-nomadic military communities and free people of Eastern Europe and the Eurasian steppe, especially associated with Russia, Ukraine, and frontier cavalry service.

parts.label: L
parts.question: These people informed Mehmed IV that he was, among other things, the “Fool of all the world and underworld, an idiot before God, [and] grandson of the Serpent.” For 10 points each:

parts.label: A
parts.question: [H] Name these semi-nomadic “free men,” who lived in Russia and Ukraine.
parts.answer: Cossacks [accept Zaporozhian Cossacks; or Kazak; or Zaporozhian host]

parts.label: B
parts.question: [M] The Cossack rebel Yemelyan Pugachev claimed to be the dead husband of this “great” Empress of Russia, and launched a rebellion. He was unsuccessful.
parts.answer: Catherine the Great [or Catherine II of Russia; or Yekaterina II Velikaya; or Sophie Friederike Auguste, Prinzessin von Anhalt-Zerbst]

parts.label: C
parts.question: [E] Catherine the Great and her actual husband, Peter III, ruled during this century. King George III came to power in England during this century.
parts.answer: 1700s [or the 18th century]

parts.label: tossup
parts.question: These people sacked the city of Astrakhan (AST-ruh-kan) during an uprising led by Stenka Razin (stain-kuh RAA-zin). In an indirect alliance with Sweden, these people revolted against the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth in the Khmelnytsky (KEL-muh-NIT-skee) Uprising to begin The Deluge. Ilya Repin (IL-yuh REP-in) painted the Zaporozhian (ZAP-uh-ROH-jin) group of these people, who sacked Kazan (kah-ZAHN) in a revolt against (*) Catherine the Great under Yemelyan Pugachev (YEM-el-yahn POOG-ah-shev). Many of these nomadic people lived around the Don and Dnieper (NEE-pur) Rivers. For 10 points, name these Slavic raiders who often served as cavalry enforcers for Russia.
parts.answer: Cossacks [or Don Cossacks; or Zaporozhian Cossacks]

topics.topic: Elizabeth II of the United Kingdom
topics.description: Elizabeth II was queen of the United Kingdom and other Commonwealth realms from 1952 until her death in 2022.

parts.label: tossup
parts.question: Marcus Sarjeant fired six blank shots at this ruler in 1981, barely managing to scare this ruler’s horse. 1992 was described as this ruler’s annus horribilis, as several extended family members had publicly reported affairs, including Sarah Ferguson and this ruler’s daughter, Princess Anne. Operation London Bridge followed the passing of, for ten points, what longest serving Queen of England, who was succeeded by Charles III after her September 2022 death?
parts.answer: Elizabeth II of the United Kingdom (accept Elizabeth Alexanda Mary Windsor; prompt on Elizabeth)

topics.description: A cultural and intellectual revival fostered by Charlemagne and his successors that advanced education, scholarship, manuscript production, the arts, and church reform.

parts.label: tossup
parts.question: This ruler’s general and brother-in-law Eric of Friuli was killed in the failed Siege of Trsat (“ter-SOT”). This ruler established the Spanish March as a buffer zone on the border of his empire. This ruler forced Widukind to convert to Christianity as part of his subjugation of the Saxons. This king had earlier defeated Desiderius in his conquest of (*) Lombardy. This subject of a biography by Einhard and son of Pepin the Short brought the scholar Alcuin of York to his court at Aachen. During his reign, this king oversaw a cultural revival named for his dynasty, the Carolingian Renaissance. For 10 points, name this Frankish king who was crowned first Holy Roman Emperor in 800.
parts.answer: Charlemagne [or Charles I or Charles the Great or Carolus Magnus or Karl der Grosse; prompt on Charles]

parts.label: tossup
parts.question: This ruler defeated Desiderius in the Siege of Pavia to become King of the Lombards in 774. From his court at Aachen, this ruler presided over the beginning of the Carolingian Renaissance. On Christmas Day 800, (*) Pope Leo III crowned this ruler as the first Holy Roman Emperor. For 10 points, name this Frankish king, who was the first to unite most of Western Europe since the fall of the Roman Empire.
parts.answer: Charlemagne [or Charles the Great or Carolus Magnus; prompt on Charles]

topics.description: The renowned Hellenistic scholarly library in Alexandria, Egypt, associated with the Ptolemaic dynasty and the preservation of extensive ancient written knowledge.

parts.label: tossup
parts.question: Due to rumors that she kept this city’s prefect, Orestes, from reconciling with its bishop, the pagan philosopher Hypatia was killed in this city by a Christian mob. At the Council of Ephesus, the primary opponent of Nestorianism was that bishop from this city, Cyril. Until it was destroyed by Theophilus, this city was home to the main temple of the cult of Serapis. After the wars of the (*) Diadochi, this city became the capital of the Ptolemaic Kingdom. A series of earthquakes destroyed a structure near this city on the island of Pharos, one of the wonders of the ancient world. For 10 points, name this Egyptian city once home to a lighthouse and a Great Library.
parts.answer: Alexandria

parts.label: tossup
parts.question: Callimachus’ lost work Pinakes [PIN-ah-keez] listed the contents of one of these locations. Legend says that, after Hulagu Khan’s 1258 siege of Baghdad, the Tigris River turned black because of the destruction of one of these places, the House of (*) Wisdom. Alexandria contained a “Great” one of, for ten points, what educational facilities that stored tablets, papyrus scrolls, or other scholarly writings?
parts.answer: library (prompt on “archive(s)”)

topics.description: A landlocked Central European country historically ruled by the Habsburgs and associated with the Austro-Hungarian Empire, Vienna, Salzburg, and the Alpine region.

parts.label: L
parts.question: Answer the following questions related to the Seven Years’ War. For 10 points each:

parts.label: A
parts.question: [E] The Diplomatic Revolution, a reversal of traditional alliances prior to the war, allied this country with France. This country was ruled by the Hapsburgs from Vienna.
parts.answer: Austria

parts.label: B
parts.question: [H] The so-called “Miracle of the House of Brandenberg” saved this ruler’s country from defeat during the war. This Prussian ruler was an enlightened despot and known for his military successes.
parts.answer: Frederick the Great [or Frederick II; prompt Frederick]

parts.label: C
parts.question: [M] The American theater of the Seven Years’ War is commonly known by this name, which references the two main enemies that the British colonists fought during the war.
parts.answer: French and Indian War

topics.description: A powerful Italian maritime republic governed by doges that dominated trade and territory in the Adriatic and eastern Mediterranean for centuries.

parts.label: tossup
parts.question: This nation-state’s leader traditionally threw a ring from the ship Bucentaur into the Adriatic to perform the annual Marriage of the Sea. This republic was led by a Doge, and its namesake capital city contains the Rialto Bridge and Saint Mark’s Basilica. Gondolas are flat-bottomed boats that help people move around, for ten points, what Most Serene Republic in modern Italy, whose namesake capital city was built over a complex of canals?
parts.answer: Republic of Venice (accept Most Serene Republic of Venice; accept Serenissima Repubblica di Venezia)

parts.label: L
parts.question: For 10 points each, answer the following about Nurbanu Sultan, the real power behind the Ottoman throne from 1574 to 1583:

parts.label: A
parts.question: [H] Nurbanu was the mother of Murad III, the successor to a sultan with this name. The first sultan with this name defeated the Safavids at the Battle of Chaldiran and destroyed the Mamluk Sultanate to conquer Egypt.
parts.answer: Selim [accept Selim I or Selim the Grim or Selim II or Selim the Sot]

parts.label: B
parts.question: [M] Nurbanu claimed to be from this polity, and she actively promoted policies benefiting this polity. The Ottomans took over the islands of Cyprus and Crete from this polity, which controlled them as part of the Stato da Mar.
parts.answer: Venice [accept Most Serene Republic of Venice or Venetian Republic]

parts.label: C
parts.question: [E] Nurbanu commissioned Mimar Sinan to construct one of these buildings in the Uskudar district of Istanbul. The Hagia Sophia was converted into one of these Muslim religious buildings after the Fall of Constantinople.
parts.answer: mosques [or masjids]

topics.description: The 1415 English victory over a much larger French army during the Hundred Years' War, achieved in muddy conditions through effective longbow tactics and defensive stakes.

parts.label: L
parts.question: Edward III began the first phase of this conflict by attempting to claim the French throne. For 10 points each:

parts.label: A
parts.question: [E] Name this lengthy conflict between the English and the French that, despite its name, lasted 116 years.
parts.answer: Hundred Years’ War

parts.label: B
parts.question: [M] During the Hundred Years’ War, this woman was inspired by several visions to take up arms and relieve the siege of Orléans. This woman was burned at the stake but canonized hundred of years later.
parts.answer: Joan of Arc [or Jeanne d'Arc or Saint Joan]

parts.label: C
parts.question: [H] The English turned the tides of war after winning this battle on Saint Crispin’s Day. English longbows played a crucial role in this victory for Henry V.
parts.answer: Battle of Agincourt <European History–Kapadia>

parts.label: tossup
parts.question: During a battle in this conflict, the strings of Genoese crossbows were weakened by rain and the blind king John of Bohemia died after tying his horse to a cavalry charge. A battle in this conflict began after a crown was stolen from a baggage train and saw its victors use wooden stakes in the muddy ground to defeat the cavalry of Charles d’Albret. That battle on St. (*) Crispin’s Day in this conflict was decided by Welsh longbowmen. A young maid lifted the siege of Orléans during this conflict, whose battles included Crécy and Agincourt. Joan of Arc helped end, for 10 points, what very lengthy war between medieval France and England?
parts.answer: ANSWER: Hundred Years’ War

topics.description: The ionic compound NaCl, commonly encountered as edible salt and naturally occurring as the mineral halite, with major historical importance as a food preservative, seasoning, and traded commodity.

parts.label: L
parts.question: A modern country named for this empire has its capital at Bamako. For ten points each,

parts.label: A
parts.question: Name this north African empire ruled by Sundiata Keita and Mansa Musa.
parts.answer: Malian Empire (accept Republic of Mali; accept Manden Kurufaba)

parts.label: B
parts.question: The Mali Empire was rich in gold and this mined, mineral resource that is essential for human life, and that is the most common food seasoning.
parts.answer: salt (accept table salt; accept rock salt; accept halite; accept sodium chloride or NaCl)

parts.label: C
parts.question: Mali traded salt and gold over this hot desert in northern Africa.
parts.answer: Sahara (accept as-sahra al-kubra)

parts.label: L
parts.question: Ibn Battuta documented much of this region’s namesake trade route, which connected West African empires to the Mediterranean Sea. For 10 points each:

parts.label: A
parts.question: Name this largest sand desert in the world, which occupies much of northern Africa.
parts.answer: Sahara Desert

parts.label: B
parts.question: Merchants from this empire and the later Songhai Empire partook in the trans-Saharan trade. This empire’s ruler Mansa Musa disrupted the Egyptian economy by handing out gold during his trip to Mecca.
parts.answer: Mali Empire

parts.label: C
parts.question: The trans-Saharan trade centered on gold and this other commodity. Much of the Songhai’s wealth came from mining this commodity at Taghaza.
parts.answer: salt
